sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Neuraxial anesthesia can avoid airway manipulation when appropriate. If general anesthesia is needed, anticipate airway edema and increased hypoxemia risk, particularly with obesity or pulmonary edema; plan skilled assistance and difficult-airway equipment.

Use a prepared airway strategy and prioritize safe, timely airway management. Video laryngoscopy is identified as an option in difficult-airway preparation; the evidence does not establish a mandatory device or endotracheal-tube size.

When general anesthesia is used, attenuate the hypertensive response to intubation while maintaining oxygenation. Select agents and technique for the individual clinical context rather than applying a fixed drug recipe.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Treat persistent severe hypertension promptly using the obstetric team’s pathway; stroke prevention is a central priority. The cited review names IV hydralazine, IV labetalol, and immediate-release oral nifedipine as commonly used agents.

Spinal sympathetic blockade and modest afterload reduction are described as generally suitable in preeclampsia, although hypotension can occur. Prevent and treat hemodynamic changes according to maternal status and the anesthetic technique.

Magnesium sulfate is used for seizure prophylaxis and treatment in severe-feature preeclampsia and eclampsia. Monitor clinical status and renal function for toxicity; use the relevant obstetric protocol rather than extrapolating a single anesthetic regimen.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: For seizure, rapidly involve the obstetric team and prioritize maternal airway and oxygenation while following the established eclampsia protocol. The supplied review identifies magnesium sulfate as the cornerstone treatment but does not provide a universal anesthesia rescue sequence.

Consider pulmonary edema when respiratory status worsens; preeclampsia-related capillary leak and cardiac dysfunction are relevant concerns. Escalate assessment and care according to the clinical presentation rather than assuming hypovolemia from oliguria alone.

HELLP may progress rapidly, including postpartum; reassess maternal condition and laboratory findings when clinically indicated. New neurologic symptoms or concern for neuraxial hematoma warrant urgent evaluation.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Pulmonary edema is a material concern, but the supplied preeclampsia review does not establish a specific perioperative fluid regimen. Individualize fluid administration to the clinical and hemodynamic context; do not apply a universal volume target.

bullets: For cesarean delivery under neuraxial anesthesia, neuraxial opioid analgesia is supported by obstetric guidance; select the technique and adjuncts for the patient and procedure rather than importing a routine regimen from an enhanced-recovery pathway.

bullets: After general anesthesia, avoid an excessive hypertensive response during emergence and maintain attention to aspiration and pulmonary-edema risk. The supplied sources do not establish detailed extubation criteria specific to preeclampsia.

Continue postanesthesia observation appropriate to maternal condition, with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. For patients with preeclampsia, postpartum management focuses particularly on elevated blood pressure.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The preeclampsia-specific source is a clinical review, not a formal guideline or comparative trial. It supports broad priorities but does not establish a complete anesthesia protocol or specific fluid, positioning, monitoring, or emergence plan.

The neuraxial thrombocytopenia consensus is the most specific supplied society guidance for platelet-related decisions, but its authors describe limited high-quality evidence and imprecise, largely observational threshold evidence. Apply its qualifiers and clinical-context framework.

General obstetric anesthesia and monitoring standards supply relevant baseline principles, but they do not resolve all severe-preeclampsia-specific choices. Enhanced-recovery recommendations primarily concern scheduled cesarean delivery and should not be treated as a disease-specific protocol.
Timing of repeat platelet testing in preeclampsia generally remains uncertain outside the specified HELLP context; local pathways and clinical evolution remain important.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Cesarean delivery may be performed with neuraxial anesthesia or general anesthesia. Neuraxial techniques are preferred for most cesarean deliveries; for urgent delivery, an existing epidural may be used instead of initiating spinal or general anesthesia, depending on the circumstances.

The dominant priorities are timely assessment of maternal and fetal status, individualized choice of anesthetic, uterine displacement until delivery, and readiness to manage hypotension, hemorrhage, inadequate anesthesia, or airway difficulty.

General anesthesia may be appropriate for some urgent maternal or fetal circumstances. The available guidance gives examples but does not establish category-specific decision-to-delivery targets or a universal threshold for choosing general anesthesia.

Recovery priorities include ongoing assessment appropriate to the anesthetic and clinical condition, and effective multimodal analgesia. When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, confirm adequate quantitative recovery before extubation.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Select the anesthetic according to maternal, obstetric, and fetal risks, patient preference, and anesthesiologist judgment. Neuraxial anesthesia is preferred for most cesarean deliveries; for urgent cases, an established epidural is one option alongside spinal or general anesthesia.

General anesthesia may be appropriate in selected emergencies, including profound fetal bradycardia, uterine rupture, severe hemorrhage or abruption, and cord prolapse. These examples do not define a mandatory technique for every case with those diagnoses.
Maintain uterine displacement, usually to the left, until delivery regardless of anesthetic technique.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: When circumstances permit, perform a focused history and examination that includes maternal and anesthetic history, relevant obstetric history, baseline blood pressure, airway, heart and lung examination, and the back when neuraxial anesthesia is planned. Significant risks warrant obstetric-anesthesia communication.

Consider aspiration risk and prophylaxis in the context of urgency and patient-specific factors. The guideline describes aspiration prophylaxis before cesarean delivery but does not establish that an elective fasting interval can be achieved before nonelective surgery.

Base platelet testing and blood-bank preparation on clinical history, examination, anticipated hemorrhagic risk, and institutional policy; routine testing or cross-match is not specified for every healthy, uncomplicated parturient.

For thrombocytopenia, weigh the risks of neuraxial procedures against general anesthesia and other clinical risks, considering etiology, bleeding history, possible disseminated intravascular coagulation, airway assessment, and patient preference; the consensus does not support a single decision rule for all patients.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: The labor-and-delivery operating suite should have resources comparable to a main operating suite, including equipment and personnel for failed intubation, inadequate anesthesia, hypotension, respiratory depression, and recovery after neuraxial or general anesthesia.
Establish and maintain IV access before neuraxial anesthesia or general anesthesia. The obstetric guideline does not require a fixed fluid volume before neuraxial anesthesia.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Cesarean delivery may be performed with neuraxial anesthesia or general anesthesia. Neuraxial techniques are preferred for most cesarean deliveries; for urgent delivery, an existing epidural may be used instead of initiating spinal or general anesthesia, depending on the circumstances.

The dominant priorities are timely assessment of maternal and fetal status, individualized choice of anesthetic, uterine displacement until delivery, and readiness to manage hypotension, hemorrhage, inadequate anesthesia, or airway difficulty.

General anesthesia may be appropriate for some urgent maternal or fetal circumstances. The available guidance gives examples but does not establish category-specific decision-to-delivery targets or a universal threshold for choosing general anesthesia.

Recovery priorities include ongoing assessment appropriate to the anesthetic and clinical condition, and effective multimodal analgesia. When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, confirm adequate quantitative recovery before extubation.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Select the anesthetic according to maternal, obstetric, and fetal risks, patient preference, and anesthesiologist judgment. Neuraxial anesthesia is preferred for most cesarean deliveries; for urgent cases, an established epidural is one option alongside spinal or general anesthesia.

General anesthesia may be appropriate in selected emergencies, including profound fetal bradycardia, uterine rupture, severe hemorrhage or abruption, and cord prolapse. These examples do not define a mandatory technique for every case with those diagnoses.
Maintain uterine displacement, usually to the left, until delivery regardless of anesthetic technique.

Consider aspiration risk and prophylaxis in the context of urgency and patient-specific factors. The guideline describes aspiration prophylaxis before cesarean delivery but does not establish that an elective fasting interval can be achieved before nonelective surgery.

Base platelet testing and blood-bank preparation on clinical history, examination, anticipated hemorrhagic risk, and institutional policy; routine testing or cross-match is not specified for every healthy, uncomplicated parturient.

For thrombocytopenia, weigh the risks of neuraxial procedures against general anesthesia and other clinical risks, considering etiology, bleeding history, possible disseminated intravascular coagulation, airway assessment, and patient preference; the consensus does not support a single decision rule for all patients.

sections.title: Obstetric airway rescue & extubation planning
bullets: Before GA, agree on aspiration risk, anticipated airway difficulty, positioning, preoxygenation, skilled help and a failed-intubation plan. Maintain uterine displacement when applicable and use head-up/ramped positioning when suitable.

Prioritize oxygenation. The OAA/DAS obstetric algorithm supports gentle mask ventilation after induction, limits repeated intubation attempts, and advises reducing or releasing cricoid pressure if it impedes ventilation or intubation.

After failed intubation, declare the problem and use facemask or an appropriate second-generation supraglottic airway for oxygenation. Decide whether to wake or proceed based on airway security, aspiration risk, maternal/fetal urgency and surgical needs.

A cannot-intubate/cannot-oxygenate emergency requires immediate escalation to emergency front-of-neck access under the trained local pathway; repeated unsuccessful instrumentation must not delay rescue.

Plan extubation and reintubation contingencies. Awake responsiveness, satisfactory ventilation/oxygenation and adequate neuromuscular recovery are prerequisites when applicable; airway edema, traumatic intubation, pulmonary edema or ongoing instability may justify continued ventilation and ICU care rather than forced extubation.

sections.title: Neuraxial morphine: dose- and risk-stratified monitoring
bullets: Assess respiratory-depression risk before selecting postoperative monitoring. Consider obesity/OSA, significant cardiopulmonary disease, chronic opioids, additional sedatives/systemic opioids, magnesium and perioperative respiratory events.

For healthy low-risk patients, SOAP’s full statement considers routine institutional cesarean monitoring sufficient after intrathecal morphine at most 0.05 mg (50 micrograms) or epidural morphine at most 1 mg. This does not mean no postoperative observation.

For healthy low-risk patients receiving intrathecal morphine greater than 0.05 through 0.15 mg (50–150 micrograms) or epidural morphine greater than 1 through 3 mg, the full SOAP statement recommends respiratory-rate and sedation assessment every two hours for 12 hours in addition to routine institutional observations.

For higher doses, SOAP directs clinicians to ASA/ASRA monitoring: at least hourly respiratory-rate and sedation assessment for the first 12 hours, then every two hours for the next 12 hours. Higher-risk patients need individualized increased intensity and consideration of oxygenation/ventilation monitoring rather than automatic low-risk scheduling.

These are monitoring dose bands, not prescribing recommendations. They apply to single-dose neuraxial morphine after cesarean, not every neuraxial opioid or continuous epidural infusion. Clinical deterioration requires immediate assessment regardless of the scheduled interval.

sections.title: Hemorrhage readiness & escalation
bullets: Match vascular access and blood preparation to placental findings, anemia, bleeding risk and the clinical course. Quantify ongoing blood loss and reassess perfusion; a normal early hemoglobin does not exclude major acute bleeding.

When PPH occurs, communicate and treat the cause while mobilizing the obstetric hemorrhage pathway, blood-bank support and appropriate resuscitation. Use the linked consolidated PPH guidance; do not wait for a fixed blood-loss number when the patient is deteriorating.

TXA for treatment of established PPH and routine prophylactic TXA are different decisions. WHO 2025 recommends early IV treatment within three hours of birth but does not recommend routine prophylactic TXA at cesarean birth.

sections.title: Urgency categories & decision-to-birth context
bullets: NICE category 1 means an immediate threat to the life of the woman or fetus; category 2 means maternal or fetal compromise that is not immediately life-threatening.
NICE advises category 1 birth as soon as possible and in most situations within 30 minutes, and category 2 as soon as possible and in most situations within 75 minutes of the decision.

These are qualified UK guideline targets, not permission to wait or a universal rule overriding maternal safety and the clinical situation. Communicate the actual emergency and agree the fastest safe anesthetic plan; category alone does not dictate GA.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Hip fracture repair may use general or neuraxial anesthesia; select the approach for the patient, fracture, comorbidities, and expected procedure rather than treating spinal anesthesia as universally superior.

Frail older adults are common in this population. Prioritize assessment of cardiovascular, respiratory, neurologic, volume, and cognitive status, and weigh the consequences of hypotension and respiratory compromise.

Neuraxial sympathectomy can cause hypotension and bradycardia; general anesthesia can worsen atelectasis and hypoxia risk. Maintain perfusion and oxygenation while anticipating technique-specific hazards, including bone cement implantation syndrome with cemented hemiarthroplasty.

Recovery priorities include adequate analgesia, early ambulation when feasible, and surveillance for respiratory or cardiovascular deterioration and altered cognition. Regional analgesia may support pain control and mobilization; it does not eliminate the need for individualized recovery monitoring.

bullets: Repair encompasses fixation or replacement for hip fractures. The supplied procedure-specific review describes both general and neuraxial anesthesia as options; choice is individualized rather than dictated by fracture repair alone.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess associated injuries and decision-making capacity, and obtain informed consent from the patient or an appropriate surrogate. Review advance directives as relevant to the anesthetic and perioperative plan.

Evaluate cardiac, pulmonary, and neurologic comorbidity, volume status, and signs of acute illness. Investigate preoperative delirium for reversible contributors rather than attributing it to age alone.

Review antithrombotic medications, coagulation status, and renal function when considering neuraxial or peripheral regional techniques. Apply current agent- and patient-specific guidance; the available sources do not justify a universal interruption schedule.

Assess for cervical spine injury or limited airway mobility where relevant; regional anesthesia may avoid airway instrumentation, but inadequate block, prolonged surgery, or major fluid shifts can require conversion to general anesthesia.

Supine positioning can reduce functional residual capacity and increase atelectasis and hypoxia risk in older adults. Incorporate respiratory status and tolerance of positioning into planning.

bullets: Neuraxial and general anesthesia are both supported options. Choose according to patient factors and procedural requirements; the supplied evidence does not support a universal airway device or a routine general-anesthesia plan.

If general anesthesia is used, account for older adults’ increased vulnerability to atelectasis, shunt, hypoxia, and hypoventilation. Tailor ventilation and airway management to the individual’s pulmonary status.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Neuraxial sympathetic blockade can reduce arterial and venous tone, lowering preload and causing hypotension or bradycardia. Maintain attention to perfusion and respond to evolving hemodynamics using the clinical context; no case-specific target is established here.

For cemented hemiarthroplasty, anticipate possible bone cement implantation syndrome around cement insertion. Acute hypotension, hypoxemia, or cardiac instability warrant prompt recognition and escalation; the supplied review describes this as a potentially serious cement-related event.

Long-bone fracture and instrumentation can be associated with fat embolism syndrome. Be alert to respiratory distress, altered mental status, and petechial rash, including delayed postoperative presentation.

Blood loss may be clinically important, but the available hip-fracture-specific summary provides no quantitative estimate or procedure-specific blood-loss protocol. Reassess hemodynamics and bleeding in context.

Neuraxial hematoma is rare but potentially devastating, and anticoagulation is an important risk factor. New neurologic concerns after neuraxial procedures require urgent evaluation; consult applicable specialty guidance.

Postoperative delirium is an important concern in this frail population, but the supplied sources do not establish a complete delirium-prevention or treatment protocol. Address contributing conditions and support early mobilization when feasible.

bullets: Repair encompasses fixation or replacement for hip fractures. The supplied procedure-specific review describes both general and neuraxial anesthesia as options; choice is individualized rather than dictated by fracture repair alone.

The older-adult fragility-fracture review favors neuraxial anesthesia when there is no contraindication, but this is not evidence that spinal anesthesia improves outcomes for every patient or procedure.

Consider regional analgesia as an adjunct or alternative for pain control, accounting for block coverage, patient cooperation, comorbidities, and potential effects of motor weakness on rehabilitation.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess associated injuries and decision-making capacity, and obtain informed consent from the patient or an appropriate surrogate. Review advance directives as relevant to the anesthetic and perioperative plan.

Evaluate cardiac, pulmonary, and neurologic comorbidity, volume status, and signs of acute illness. Investigate preoperative delirium for reversible contributors rather than attributing it to age alone.

Review antithrombotic medications, coagulation status, and renal function when considering neuraxial or peripheral regional techniques. Apply current agent- and patient-specific guidance; the available sources do not justify a universal interruption schedule.

Assess for cervical spine injury or limited airway mobility where relevant; regional anesthesia may avoid airway instrumentation, but inadequate block, prolonged surgery, or major fluid shifts can require conversion to general anesthesia.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: The supplied hip-fracture procedure summary does not specify table configuration, fluoroscopy, vascular access, or catheter setup. Choose these with the surgical team for the planned fracture repair; do not infer a universal setup from this evidence.
Supine positioning can reduce functional residual capacity and increase atelectasis and hypoxia risk in older adults. Incorporate respiratory status and tolerance of positioning into planning.

Apply basic anesthetic monitoring appropriate to the technique: continuously evaluate oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; display ECG and assess blood pressure and heart rate at least every five minutes. Use additional monitoring when clinically indicated.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Neuraxial and general anesthesia are both supported options. Choose according to patient factors and procedural requirements; the supplied evidence does not support a universal airway device or a routine general-anesthesia plan.

If general anesthesia is used, account for older adults’ increased vulnerability to atelectasis, shunt, hypoxia, and hypoventilation. Tailor ventilation and airway management to the individual’s pulmonary status.

For general anesthesia, verify airway-device position and use the required ventilation monitoring. During moderate or deep sedation, evaluate ventilation clinically and monitor expired carbon dioxide unless patient, procedure, or equipment prevents it.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Neuraxial sympathetic blockade can reduce arterial and venous tone, lowering preload and causing hypotension or bradycardia. Maintain attention to perfusion and respond to evolving hemodynamics using the clinical context; no case-specific target is established here.

For cemented hemiarthroplasty, anticipate possible bone cement implantation syndrome around cement insertion. Acute hypotension, hypoxemia, or cardiac instability warrant prompt recognition and escalation; the supplied review describes this as a potentially serious cement-related event.

Long-bone fracture and instrumentation can be associated with fat embolism syndrome. Be alert to respiratory distress, altered mental status, and petechial rash, including delayed postoperative presentation.

Blood loss may be clinically important, but the available hip-fracture-specific summary provides no quantitative estimate or procedure-specific blood-loss protocol. Reassess hemodynamics and bleeding in context.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: For sudden unexplained hypotension, refractory tachycardia, syncope, or hypoxemia, consider serious causes including pulmonary embolism in the hip/pelvic surgery context and escalate assessment and support. The source does not establish a single diagnostic or treatment algorithm.

Neuraxial hematoma is rare but potentially devastating, and anticoagulation is an important risk factor. New neurologic concerns after neuraxial procedures require urgent evaluation; consult applicable specialty guidance.

Postoperative delirium is an important concern in this frail population, but the supplied sources do not establish a complete delirium-prevention or treatment protocol. Address contributing conditions and support early mobilization when feasible.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: Optimize volume status before anesthesia because hypovolemia can magnify cardiovascular effects of anesthetic drugs. The source supports individualized assessment, not a fixed pre-load or total fluid volume.

With neuraxial hypotension, reduced preload from venodilation may be relevant; fluid bolus and vasopressors are described as possible responses. Select management according to the patient’s hemodynamics and comorbidities.

Neuraxial anesthesia is associated with reduced intraoperative blood loss in the review, but the provided sources give no hip-fracture-specific transfusion threshold or blood-loss replacement regimen.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Consider fascia iliaca or femoral regional analgesia to improve pain control and facilitate mobilization. Select the approach with attention to anticoagulation, block-related risks, and rehabilitation needs.

Use multimodal postoperative analgesia and avoid undertreating pain, which may impede ambulation and prolong recovery. The older-adult review identifies acetaminophen as a likely first-line option when hepatic function is normal; individualize other agents to patient risks.

Regional anesthesia has been associated with reduced postoperative nausea and vomiting compared with general anesthesia using volatile agents, but the evidence does not establish a patient-specific PONV regimen.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: The supplied hip-fracture procedure source does not specify an emergence protocol. After general anesthesia, assess recovery and airway readiness according to the anesthetic and patient condition.

If neuromuscular blocking drugs were used, use quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirm recovery before extubation; this recommendation applies to cases using neuromuscular blockade, not to local or neuraxial anesthesia without it.

In PACU or equivalent care, continually assess the patient, with attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. Support early mobilization as clinically appropriate and monitor for evolving respiratory, cardiac, neurologic, or thromboembolic concerns.

sections.title: Cementation: team preparation & vigilance
bullets: Before femoral-canal instrumentation and cement insertion, identify heightened cardiopulmonary risk, agree team roles and ensure the surgeon’s warning is heard and acknowledged. Have vasoactive support immediately available and correct hypovolemia without indiscriminate fluid loading.

The 2015 joint safety guideline for cemented hemiarthroplasty calls for close blood-pressure monitoring during and shortly after cementation, with invasive monitoring in higher-risk patients. A sudden fall in pressure or end-tidal CO₂ under GA may signal right-heart failure or a major fall in cardiac output.

That guideline advises systolic pressure within 20% of the pre-induction value in its setting. This is source-specific guidance, not a universal target for all arthroplasty patients or a substitute for assessing perfusion and the patient’s baseline.

New hypoxemia, hypotension or cardiovascular collapse around instrumentation, cementation or prosthesis insertion requires immediate communication, resuscitation and evaluation for BCIS and other causes. The prevention guideline is not a complete stand-alone cardiac-arrest algorithm.

The guideline’s direct focus is cemented hemiarthroplasty for hip fracture. Applying its team-preparation principles to other cemented arthroplasty requires procedural and patient context; it does not choose the implant or mandate uncemented surgery.

sections.title: Neuraxial/deep-block & thromboprophylaxis coordination
bullets: Before neuraxial or deep plexus/peripheral procedures, identify the exact anticoagulant or antiplatelet drug, dose, last administration, renal function and additional bleeding risks. Use current ASRA drug-specific guidance rather than a single interval for every agent.

Coordinate catheter removal and the first postoperative anticoagulant dose before handoff. Surgical hemostasis, dose intensity and neuraxial timing all matter; catheter removal is itself a bleeding-risk event.

Do not stop clinically indicated antithrombotic treatment independently or delay urgent surgery solely to obtain a preferred anesthetic technique. Discuss feasible anesthetic alternatives and the bleeding/thrombosis tradeoff with the treating team.

bullets: Long-bone fracture fixation may use open reduction and internal fixation with plates or an intramedullary nail; the sources do not establish one approach as usual across tibia, femur, and humerus fractures.

sections.title: Lower-leg trauma: analgesia & compartment surveillance
bullets: For tibial/lower-leg injury, identify acute compartment syndrome risk and agree a multidisciplinary surveillance and escalation plan. Observations should occur at defined intervals by trained staff, with equipment and a pathway for compartment-pressure measurement when indicated.

Offer effective analgesia; regional analgesia is not universally prohibited. The 2021 guideline advises avoiding dense regional blocks whose duration substantially exceeds surgery and describes lower-concentration peripheral blocks without adjuncts as an option only with appropriate, effective surveillance.

Increasing pain or pain on passive stretch can be concerning, but severe pain is not always present. Do not wait for pulselessness or paralysis, which are late signs, or use apparent comfort under a block to exclude compartment syndrome.

When the examination is unreliable or the diagnosis remains uncertain, obtain urgent surgical assessment and use compartment-pressure measurement as appropriate. No single sign or test guarantees exclusion.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Arthroscopic rotator cuff repair addresses partial- or full-thickness tears; the operation and its duration vary with tear size, acuity, associated pathology, and repair complexity.
General anesthesia combined with regional analgesia is a common approach for significant, longer repairs; beach-chair and lateral-decubitus positioning are both used.

Priorities include protecting cerebral perfusion in the beach-chair position, anticipating interscalene-related diaphragmatic impairment, and detecting irrigation-fluid extravasation that may threaten the airway.
Plan recovery around airway reassessment when extravasation is suspected and sustained multimodal analgesia to support rehabilitation; use opioids as rescue rather than the sole analgesic strategy.

In beach-chair positioning, anticipate hypotension, bradycardia, and reduced cerebral perfusion; respond promptly to blood-pressure falls while accounting for the pressure gradient between the heart and brain.

Use basic anesthetic monitoring. Arterial pressure monitoring and cerebral oximetry are not established as obligatory for every repair; individualize additional monitoring to patient risk and clinical circumstances.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Beach-chair positioning can reduce cerebral perfusion and cause hypotension or bradycardia. Maintain vigilance through positioning and surgery; avoid deliberate hypotension as a routine analgesic strategy.

Arthroscopic irrigation creates a specific airway hazard: extravasated fluid may produce neck or mediastinal swelling, airway edema, or tracheal compression. Risk increases with prolonged surgery, poor positioning, high irrigation pressure, and obesity.
Track irrigation fluid used and collected, and follow airway pressure/compliance and neck swelling when extravasation is a concern. Consider a cuff-leak assessment before extubation in that context.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Suspected cerebral hypoperfusion in beach-chair positioning warrants prompt assessment of hemodynamics, head/neck position, and oxygenation, with escalation according to the clinical situation; the available sources do not establish a universal pressure target.

New neck swelling, rising airway pressures, or concern for airway obstruction after substantial irrigation should prompt reassessment before extubation and readiness to manage airway compromise. Do not treat extubation as routine when edema is suspected.
After interscalene block, assess dyspnea in the context of possible hemidiaphragmatic paresis; block selection should account for respiratory reserve.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Use multimodal analgesia unless contraindicated: paracetamol and an NSAID or COX-2-specific inhibitor, with opioids reserved for rescue. Individualize agents to patient factors and local practice.

Offer single-shot or continuous interscalene block as first-choice regional analgesia when appropriate; the guideline discussion favors continuous block, while diaphragm-sparing alternatives may be considered when interscalene block is unsuitable.

A single-shot block may wear off with rebound pain; maintain regular non-opioid analgesia through that transition. Intravenous dexamethasone is recommended by the guideline to prolong block analgesia and provide antiemetic effects.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Before extubation, reassess for irrigation-related airway edema when there is neck swelling or other concern; use airway pressure/compliance, neck assessment, and cuff-leak evaluation as relevant to the clinical picture.

When neuromuscular blocking drugs have been used, use quantitative monitoring and confirm adequate recovery at the adductor pollicis before extubation; this requirement does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

Provide postanesthesia observation appropriate to the patient's condition, including attention to oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature; reassess pain and respiratory symptoms.

sections.title: Evidence scope & limitations
bullets: The principal perioperative source is a current-concept review, not a trial or formal guideline. The procedure-specific pain guideline is based on randomized trials but reports heterogeneous studies and did not perform a meta-analysis.

Beach-chair blood-pressure statements differ in specificity across sources. The shoulder review emphasizes rapid treatment of hypotension; another orthopedic review reports a study-specific cerebral blood-flow observation. These do not establish one universal target for every patient or procedure.
The evidence does not establish a universal irrigation-fluid balance, IV fluid total, blood-loss threshold, arterial-line indication, or beach-chair pressure target for all rotator cuff repairs.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Arthroscopic rotator cuff repair addresses partial- or full-thickness tears; the operation and its duration vary with tear size, acuity, associated pathology, and repair complexity.
General anesthesia combined with regional analgesia is a common approach for significant, longer repairs; beach-chair and lateral-decubitus positioning are both used.

Priorities include protecting cerebral perfusion in the beach-chair position, anticipating interscalene-related diaphragmatic impairment, and detecting irrigation-fluid extravasation that may threaten the airway.
Plan recovery around airway reassessment when extravasation is suspected and sustained multimodal analgesia to support rehabilitation; use opioids as rescue rather than the sole analgesic strategy.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Repair may be arthroscopic or open; the procedure-specific guideline recommends an arthroscopic approach whenever possible because it is associated with less postoperative pain.
The operation may involve partial or complete repair, debridement with acromioplasty, or graft-based reconstruction; choices depend on tear characteristics and patient factors.
Significant tears may require longer, more complex surgery. Anticipated duration and complexity should inform the anesthetic technique and analgesia plan.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess comorbidities and cardiorespiratory reserve, age, tear acuity and size, associated injuries, anticoagulation, and positioning/analgesia needs. For traumatic tears, assess for other injuries.

Before interscalene block, consider pulmonary reserve and pre-existing diaphragmatic dysfunction because phrenic involvement can impair respiratory function. Discuss alternatives when that risk is clinically important.
Agree on positioning and regional technique with the patient, surgeon, and anesthesiologist after weighing block coverage, duration, adverse effects, and rehabilitation implications.

sections.title: Beach-chair position: pressure at the brain
bullets: When the head is above the arm cuff, arm pressure overestimates pressure at the brain. Account for the vertical hydrostatic gradient; with an arterial line, use an explicitly documented brain-level reference such as the external auditory meatus rather than silently treating heart-level MAP as brain-level MAP.

Avoid deliberate hypotension for surgical visualization in the beach-chair position. The APSF safety review favors pressure close to the patient’s awake baseline, with prompt correction of hypotension and attention to oxygenation, ventilation and head position.

This safety review does not establish a single validated brain-MAP threshold for every patient. Do not transplant a study-specific number or a routine supine MAP target into this setting without considering the measurement level, baseline pressure and cerebrovascular risk.

sources.label: APSF: blood pressure in the beach-chair position (2020 safety review)

sections.title: Irrigation extravasation & extubation reassessment
bullets: Watch for neck, face or chest swelling and changes in airway pressure or compliance during shoulder arthroscopy. Draping should permit appropriate observation of the neck and nearby chest when feasible.

Examine for extravasation and airway compromise before extubation. If significant edema is present, consider continued intubation and monitored postoperative care until the airway can be managed safely; do not assume completion of surgery means the airway is ready.
If the airway is not already secured, progressive neck swelling can make later intubation difficult. Escalate early when swelling or respiratory compromise develops.

The systematic review is dominated by case reports and small series. Its reported resolution times, pump settings and interventions are not validated universal thresholds, and it cannot establish a routine complication rate.

sections.title: Evidence scope & focused safety supplementation
bullets: The October 7 update supplements this draft with the focused safety references linked in the new sections. These address selected historical review gaps, not every aspect of perioperative care.

Existing procedure reviews remain limited by their study populations, study designs and variable evidence quality. A preference reported in a review is not a mandate for one airway device, anesthetic technique, block or recovery pathway.

Keep source-specific populations distinct: lower-leg compartment guidance is not a universal all-fracture protocol; cemented hemiarthroplasty guidance is not a universal implant-selection rule; a beach-chair safety review does not establish one blood-pressure target for every patient.

Patient-specific decisions, the remaining historical review questions and independent clinical signoff remain open. No universal drug, fluid, transfusion or disposition recipe has been inferred from missing procedure-specific evidence.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Shoulder arthroplasty may be performed with general anesthesia, regional anesthesia, or a combination; interscalene block is a commonly described regional technique, but the choice must reflect patient and procedural factors.

For beach-chair positioning, prioritize cerebral perfusion and recognize that apparently stable routine vital signs may not exclude reduced cerebral oxygenation; available blood-pressure findings are review-level, not a universal target.
Interscalene block can provide substantial analgesia, but phrenic nerve effects and other block complications matter, particularly when pulmonary reserve is limited.

Plan recovery around respiratory assessment, effective analgesia as the block resolves, and appropriate postanesthesia observation; no shoulder-arthroplasty-specific emergence or PACU regimen is established in these sources.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: Shoulder arthroplasty includes total, reverse, hemiarthroplasty, and revision procedures. The supplied sources identify these procedure types but do not provide a surgical approach or implant-selection protocol.

Anesthetic options include regional anesthesia, general anesthesia, or a combination. Interscalene block is described for total shoulder arthroplasty and proximal humeral prosthetic replacement; selection depends on coverage, patient factors, and the planned operation.

Regional anesthesia combined with general anesthesia is supported as an option, not a mandatory technique: the arthroplasty review favors the combination while reporting variable results across studies.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess cardiopulmonary reserve, cardiovascular disease, anemia, comorbidity burden, and factors that may increase postoperative medical risk; arrange specialty review or optimization when indicated by the patient’s condition.

Clarify neurologic, pulmonary, and cardiovascular history before considering an upper-extremity block. In particular, assess pulmonary function where phrenic involvement could be consequential; pre-existing diaphragmatic dysfunction is also relevant.

Review antithrombotic therapy, coagulation status, and pre-existing neurologic disease when regional techniques are contemplated. Apply current, relevant specialty guidance to the actual block and medication rather than using a generic interval from this reference.
Discuss the benefits and risks of regional anesthesia, including block failure and respiratory effects, and agree on alternatives for intraoperative anesthesia and postoperative pain control.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Beach-chair positioning is associated with reduced cerebral oxygenation and perfusion in the available review. Positioning protocols, head fixation details, and a universal blood-pressure correction for the arm-to-brain gradient are not specified by these sources.

If beach-chair positioning is used, consider cerebral oximetry as an adjunct and establish a baseline before positioning when feasible. The supplied beach-chair review describes continuous cerebral oximetry and a relative alert threshold; it does not establish NIRS as mandatory for every case.

Use standard anesthetic monitoring appropriate to the anesthetic. ASA basic standards require ECG display, blood pressure and heart-rate assessment at least every five minutes, and oxygenation assessment during anesthesia.

Consider invasive arterial monitoring based on individual cardiovascular or cerebrovascular risk and the need for reliable pressure monitoring; the sources do not support a routine arterial line for all shoulder arthroplasties.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: The available sources do not establish a preferred airway device, routine use of a laryngeal mask, or a specific ventilation strategy for shoulder arthroplasty. Choose an airway approach according to the anesthetic, patient, and positioning.

For general anesthesia, follow basic monitoring standards for ventilation and confirm airway-device position with clinical assessment and expired carbon dioxide. During moderate or deep sedation, use expired-carbon-dioxide monitoring unless the patient, procedure, or equipment precludes it.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Avoid hypotension that could compromise cerebral perfusion during beach-chair positioning. One study summarized in a 2025 clinical review suggested cerebral blood flow was maintained above a particular MAP; that finding is not a universal patient-specific target or a procedure guideline.

The beach-chair review describes gradual table elevation and attention to venous return as measures discussed for perfusion management. Their use should be individualized; the shoulder-arthroplasty complication review provides no specific physiologic protocol.

Cerebral desaturation or suspected neurologic compromise warrants prompt assessment of pressure, oxygenation, and head position, with escalation to the anesthesia and surgical team. The source describes these as responses to desaturation, not a complete rescue algorithm.
Routine blood-loss expectations, specific critical surgical phases, and a standard hemodynamic protocol for arthroplasty are not provided in the procedure-specific sources.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: Interscalene block can cause hemidiaphragmatic paresis, Horner syndrome, hoarseness, and other complications; respiratory consequences depend on the patient’s reserve. New dyspnea requires clinical assessment rather than automatic attribution to the block.

Other reported block hazards include local-anesthetic systemic toxicity, pneumothorax, venous air embolism, and neurologic injury. Maintain appropriate monitoring and readiness to escalate; the incidence figures in the review are not a shoulder-arthroplasty-specific risk estimate.

Medical complications after shoulder arthroplasty vary across studies and include cardiovascular, genitourinary, respiratory, and thromboembolic events. Risk assessment should account for indication and comorbidity, rather than treating a pooled rate as an individual prediction.

For suspected serious cardiopulmonary or neurologic events, recognize the deterioration, summon appropriate help, and follow applicable institutional emergency pathways; these sources do not establish a shoulder-specific resuscitation algorithm.

sections.title: Fluids, bleeding & perfusion
bullets: The supplied arthroplasty review does not provide a typical blood-loss estimate, fluid prescription, transfusion threshold, or case-specific blood-product preparation rule. Individualize these decisions to patient risk, procedure, and observed bleeding.

Transfusion is reported in heterogeneous arthroplasty cohorts, and transfused patients often had greater comorbidity and longer operative times; the review does not establish that transfusion itself causes the associated complications.

For major procedures with substantial blood loss or fluid shifts, the orthopedic blood-pressure review discusses goal-directed fluid therapy. It does not supply a shoulder-arthroplasty-specific fluid volume or mandate that approach for every case.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Interscalene block is a regional analgesic option for shoulder surgery. The review presents multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesia as necessary and describes continuous interscalene infusion as its preferred technique for most shoulder-surgery patients, with catheters indicated in almost all open procedures, particularly rotator-cuff repair. These are review conclusions, not a universal protocol.

Single-shot block duration is finite, and pain may increase as it regresses. Ensure a transition plan using appropriate non-opioid and rescue analgesia; the supplied sources do not establish a specific arthroplasty medication regimen or dose.

Consider block alternatives when phrenic nerve effects are undesirable. The review describes suprascapular with or without axillary nerve block as less likely to cause phrenic blockade, while noting that analgesia may be inferior to interscalene block.
No shoulder-arthroplasty-specific PONV prevention regimen is provided in the fetched sources; assess and manage PONV according to the patient and applicable local guidance.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: No procedure-specific emergence or extubation approach is supplied. If neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, quantitative monitoring at the adductor pollicis and confirmation of TOF ratio at least 0.9 before extubation follow the cited ASA guideline summary.

Provide postanesthesia care with ongoing assessment appropriate to condition, including oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature. Pulse oximetry is required during the initial phase of recovery under the cited standard, subject to its stated exception and waiver provisions.

Assess respiratory symptoms in the context of the block and the patient’s pulmonary reserve, and provide analgesia as the block regresses. The shoulder-surgery review does not provide a specific PACU observation duration or discharge protocol.
Transport and handoff should preserve monitoring and support appropriate to the patient’s condition, with transfer of the perioperative course to the receiving nurse.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: Interscalene block is a regional analgesic option for shoulder surgery. Single-shot block duration is finite, and pain may increase as it regresses. Ensure a transition plan using appropriate non-opioid and rescue analgesia; the supplied sources do not establish a specific arthroplasty medication regimen or dose.

Consider block alternatives when phrenic nerve effects are undesirable. The review describes suprascapular with or without axillary nerve block as less likely to cause phrenic blockade, while noting that analgesia may be inferior to interscalene block.

bullets: Shoulder arthroscopy may be performed with regional anesthesia, sedation, or general anesthesia; patients may be positioned sitting or lateral. Select the anesthetic and airway approach for the operation, patient, and positioning rather than assuming one standard technique.

bullets: Do not infer a mandatory endotracheal tube for beach-chair cases or a laryngeal mask for lateral cases from these sources. Airway choice depends on the intended anesthetic, patient, surgical access, and the ability to manage airway complications.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Treat beach-chair elevation as a cerebral-perfusion risk, particularly in older patients or those with cerebrovascular disease. Expect that interscalene block may impair ipsilateral diaphragmatic function. Respiratory impact varies with technique and volume; monitor clinically and do not assume a low-volume approach will preserve function in every patient with limited reserve.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: If neck or chest swelling, respiratory distress, or concern for airway compression develops, recognize possible irrigation-fluid extravasation and escalate airway evaluation and support. Case reports establish a serious hazard, not its routine incidence or a single rescue pathway.

Assess respiratory symptoms after interscalene block in light of expected phrenic involvement, but do not dismiss significant or worsening dyspnea as routine. Pneumothorax is also a recognized, uncommon block complication.

For inadequate block or unexpected neurologic symptoms, reassess block effect and consider alternative analgesia or conversion as clinically indicated. Block-related neurologic injury is uncommon but may be serious; the sources do not define a shoulder-arthroscopy-specific troubleshooting algorithm.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: THA replaces the hip joint and may be performed through different surgical approaches; neuraxial anesthesia is generally favored for primary unilateral THA when no important contraindication or special circumstance precludes it, with GA or combined techniques remaining options.

Priorities include anticipating hemodynamic change with neuraxial block and, for cemented arthroplasty, recognizing possible bone cement implantation syndrome (BCIS); maintain vigilance during key surgical phases and escalate promptly if instability develops.
Blood conservation and individualized VTE prevention are important. Tranexamic acid is supported in THA, while prophylaxis choice and duration depend on patient factors and surgical preference.
Recovery is organized around pain and nausea control, resolution of motor and sympathetic block, safe mobilization, VTE prevention, and coordinated discharge planning.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: THA is an operation for hip-joint replacement. Surgical approach and implant choice vary; the available review does not establish one approach as superior within an ERAS pathway. Severe deformity or stiffness may require more extensive soft-tissue release and affect early pain and mobilization.

Direct anterior surgery is described as muscle-sparing, but cited evidence did not show better early mobilization, pain, length of stay, or outcome than the posterior approach within ERAS. Robotic assistance can add workflow and duration considerations, particularly during the learning curve.

Cemented and uncemented implants have different early recovery trajectories. Confirm the planned approach and whether cementing is expected with the surgical team because cement insertion is a relevant hemodynamic risk phase.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess medical status and develop an anesthesia plan in light of comorbidity, patient preference, and the planned operation. For primary unilateral THA, consensus favors neuraxial anesthesia when there is no significant contraindication or special circumstance; the decision remains individualized.

Review antithrombotic therapy, coagulation status, and the intended neuraxial or peripheral technique together. The regional-anesthesia review advises following applicable antithrombotic guidance; its reproduced timing table should not substitute for current, patient-specific guidance.
Identify and address anemia early, investigate its cause, and coordinate treatment to reduce avoidable delay and transfusion risk. Risk-assess all patients for VTE before surgery.

Consider smoking and alcohol history, fasting, and the planned recovery pathway as part of preparation. ERAS emphasizes multidisciplinary coordination and consistent patient information; the benefit and format of home-based prehabilitation remain uncertain.

bullets: Neuraxial anesthesia is recommended by the ICAROS consensus for primary unilateral THA when no important contraindication or special circumstance precludes it. The recommendation is supported by low-to-moderate evidence and does not specify a single spinal drug, dose, or anesthetic recipe.

Neuraxial anesthesia was associated with lower odds of several adverse outcomes than GA in pooled THA data, including DVT/PE and transfusion; urinary retention was more frequent. These are group-level associations, not guarantees for an individual.

The THA sources do not prescribe an airway device or ventilation strategy. If GA, sedation, or a supraglottic airway is used, apply general standards appropriate to the anesthetic and patient; during moderate or deep sedation, assess ventilation and monitor expired carbon dioxide unless precluded or invalidated.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Neuraxial sympathetic block can cause hypotension and orthostatic intolerance; residual block can delay standing and mobilization. Select technique and recovery timing with the intended early-mobilization pathway in mind.

During cement insertion, watch for abrupt hypotension, hypoxemia, arrhythmia, or cardiovascular collapse. The supplied clinical review describes marrow debris and cement monomer-related pathways; alert the team and escalate promptly if instability occurs.

Fat embolism syndrome may complicate long-bone fractures, intramedullary nailing, or joint arthroplasty. Its classic features are respiratory distress, altered mental status, and petechial rash; onset is typically 12–72 hours after injury or instrumentation.

Coordinate the timing of surgery, neuraxial block, and equipment changes. Robotic learning curves or moving equipment can prolong workflow and may affect whether neuraxial anesthesia remains adequate through closure.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: BCIS can progress rapidly to right-ventricular failure, systemic vasodilation, and cardiac arrest. Recognize the temporal relationship to cement insertion, communicate with the surgical team, and escalate hemodynamic support according to the institution's emergency response; the supplied review is not a society protocol.

Consider pulmonary embolism with sudden unexplained hypotension, refractory tachycardia, or syncope in the perioperative hip/pelvic-surgery setting. Hypoxemia and pleuritic chest pain may follow; escalate assessment and management urgently.

After neuraxial anesthesia, hypotension, urinary retention, and delayed mobilization are relevant recovery concerns. Assess the clinical state and block resolution; do not equate an apparently recovered motor block with readiness to mobilize safely.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: THA replaces the hip joint and may be performed through different surgical approaches; neuraxial anesthesia is generally favored for primary unilateral THA when no important contraindication or special circumstance precludes it, with GA or combined techniques remaining options.

Priorities include anticipating hemodynamic change with neuraxial block and, for cemented arthroplasty, recognizing possible bone cement implantation syndrome (BCIS); maintain vigilance during key surgical phases and escalate promptly if instability develops.
Blood conservation and individualized VTE prevention are important. Tranexamic acid is supported in THA, while prophylaxis choice and duration depend on patient factors and surgical preference.
Recovery is organized around pain and nausea control, resolution of motor and sympathetic block, safe mobilization, VTE prevention, and coordinated discharge planning.

sections.title: Procedure & approach
bullets: THA is an operation for hip-joint replacement. Surgical approach and implant choice vary; the available review does not establish one approach as superior within an ERAS pathway. Severe deformity or stiffness may require more extensive soft-tissue release and affect early pain and mobilization.

Direct anterior surgery is described as muscle-sparing, but cited evidence did not show better early mobilization, pain, length of stay, or outcome than the posterior approach within ERAS. Robotic assistance can add workflow and duration considerations, particularly during the learning curve.

Cemented and uncemented implants have different early recovery trajectories. Confirm the planned approach and whether cementing is expected with the surgical team because cement insertion is a relevant hemodynamic risk phase.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & risk modifiers
bullets: Assess medical status and develop an anesthesia plan in light of comorbidity, patient preference, and the planned operation. For primary unilateral THA, consensus favors neuraxial anesthesia when there is no significant contraindication or special circumstance; the decision remains individualized.

Review antithrombotic therapy, coagulation status, and the intended neuraxial or peripheral technique together. The regional-anesthesia review advises following applicable antithrombotic guidance; its reproduced timing table should not substitute for current, patient-specific guidance.
Identify and address anemia early, investigate its cause, and coordinate treatment to reduce avoidable delay and transfusion risk. Risk-assess all patients for VTE before surgery.

Consider smoking and alcohol history, fasting, and the planned recovery pathway as part of preparation. ERAS emphasizes multidisciplinary coordination and consistent patient information; the benefit and format of home-based prehabilitation remain uncertain.

sections.title: Room setup, positioning & monitoring
bullets: Positioning depends on the surgical approach and local technique. The available THA review gives no standard positioning protocol; coordinate positioning and equipment needs with the surgical team, including any robotic or image-intensification workflow.

Apply the applicable basic anesthetic monitoring standards: qualified anesthesia personnel remain present, and oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature are continually evaluated. Blood pressure and heart rate are assessed at least every five minutes; add monitoring according to clinical circumstances.

A THA-specific review does not establish routine arterial access or other special monitoring for every patient. Consider invasive monitoring in context of individual disease and anticipated hemodynamic risk rather than treating it as universal.

sections.title: Airway, technique & ventilation
bullets: Neuraxial anesthesia is recommended by the ICAROS consensus for primary unilateral THA when no important contraindication or special circumstance precludes it. The recommendation is supported by low-to-moderate evidence and does not specify a single spinal drug, dose, or anesthetic recipe.

Neuraxial anesthesia was associated with lower odds of several adverse outcomes than GA in pooled THA data, including DVT/PE and transfusion; urinary retention was more frequent. These are group-level associations, not guarantees for an individual.

The THA sources do not prescribe an airway device or ventilation strategy. If GA, sedation, or a supraglottic airway is used, apply general standards appropriate to the anesthetic and patient; during moderate or deep sedation, assess ventilation and monitor expired carbon dioxide unless precluded or invalidated.

When neuromuscular blocking drugs are used, use quantitative monitoring rather than clinical assessment alone and confirm adequate recovery at the adductor pollicis before extubation. This does not apply to cases without neuromuscular blockade.

sections.title: Intraoperative physiology & critical phases
bullets: Neuraxial sympathetic block can cause hypotension and orthostatic intolerance; residual block can delay standing and mobilization. Select technique and recovery timing with the intended early-mobilization pathway in mind.

During cement insertion, watch for abrupt hypotension, hypoxemia, arrhythmia, or cardiovascular collapse. The supplied clinical review describes marrow debris and cement monomer-related pathways; alert the team and escalate promptly if instability occurs.

Fat embolism syndrome may complicate long-bone fractures, intramedullary nailing, or joint arthroplasty. Its classic features are respiratory distress, altered mental status, and petechial rash; onset is typically 12–72 hours after injury or instrumentation.

Coordinate the timing of surgery, neuraxial block, and equipment changes. Robotic learning curves or moving equipment can prolong workflow and may affect whether neuraxial anesthesia remains adequate through closure.

sections.title: Complications & troubleshooting
bullets: BCIS can progress rapidly to right-ventricular failure, systemic vasodilation, and cardiac arrest. Recognize the temporal relationship to cement insertion, communicate with the surgical team, and escalate hemodynamic support according to the institution's emergency response; the supplied review is not a society protocol.

Consider pulmonary embolism with sudden unexplained hypotension, refractory tachycardia, or syncope in the perioperative hip/pelvic-surgery setting. Hypoxemia and pleuritic chest pain may follow; escalate assessment and management urgently.

After neuraxial anesthesia, hypotension, urinary retention, and delayed mobilization are relevant recovery concerns. Assess the clinical state and block resolution; do not equate an apparently recovered motor block with readiness to mobilize safely.

sections.title: Cementation: team preparation & vigilance
bullets: Before femoral-canal instrumentation and cement insertion, identify heightened cardiopulmonary risk, agree team roles and ensure the surgeon’s warning is heard and acknowledged. Have vasoactive support immediately available and correct hypovolemia without indiscriminate fluid loading.

The 2015 joint safety guideline for cemented hemiarthroplasty calls for close blood-pressure monitoring during and shortly after cementation, with invasive monitoring in higher-risk patients. A sudden fall in pressure or end-tidal CO₂ under GA may signal right-heart failure or a major fall in cardiac output.

That guideline advises systolic pressure within 20% of the pre-induction value in its setting. This is source-specific guidance, not a universal target for all arthroplasty patients or a substitute for assessing perfusion and the patient’s baseline.

New hypoxemia, hypotension or cardiovascular collapse around instrumentation, cementation or prosthesis insertion requires immediate communication, resuscitation and evaluation for BCIS and other causes. The prevention guideline is not a complete stand-alone cardiac-arrest algorithm.

The guideline’s direct focus is cemented hemiarthroplasty for hip fracture. Applying its team-preparation principles to other cemented arthroplasty requires procedural and patient context; it does not choose the implant or mandate uncemented surgery.

sections.title: Neuraxial/deep-block & thromboprophylaxis coordination
bullets: Before neuraxial or deep plexus/peripheral procedures, identify the exact anticoagulant or antiplatelet drug, dose, last administration, renal function and additional bleeding risks. Use current ASRA drug-specific guidance rather than a single interval for every agent.

Coordinate catheter removal and the first postoperative anticoagulant dose before handoff. Surgical hemostasis, dose intensity and neuraxial timing all matter; catheter removal is itself a bleeding-risk event.

Do not stop clinically indicated antithrombotic treatment independently or delay urgent surgery solely to obtain a preferred anesthetic technique. Discuss feasible anesthetic alternatives and the bleeding/thrombosis tradeoff with the treating team.

sections.title: Evidence scope & focused safety supplementation
bullets: The October 7 update supplements this draft with the focused safety references linked in the new sections. These address selected historical review gaps, not every aspect of perioperative care.

Existing procedure reviews remain limited by their study populations, study designs and variable evidence quality. A preference reported in a review is not a mandate for one airway device, anesthetic technique, block or recovery pathway.

Keep source-specific populations distinct: lower-leg compartment guidance is not a universal all-fracture protocol; cemented hemiarthroplasty guidance is not a universal implant-selection rule; a beach-chair safety review does not establish one blood-pressure target for every patient.

Patient-specific decisions, the remaining historical review questions and independent clinical signoff remain open. No universal drug, fluid, transfusion or disposition recipe has been inferred from missing procedure-specific evidence.

bullets: The TKA review reports lower transfusion requirements with neuraxial anesthesia in some studies, while cited meta-analyses found insufficient evidence for a blood-loss difference. Interpret these as comparative findings, not a patient-specific transfusion or fluid protocol.

Maintain attention to perfusion when tourniquet release may produce hypotension. The orthopedic blood-pressure review discusses limb-tourniquet physiology generally, not a TKA-specific fluid prescription.

A specific TKA fluid regimen, blood-loss estimate, transfusion threshold, and tranexamic-acid protocol are not established by the supplied TKA source material; individualize using clinical context and applicable local guidance.

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV
bullets: ACB is a sensory-selective option associated with less quadriceps impairment than femoral nerve block and may support earlier mobilization. Comparisons across studies have limitations, so analgesic adequacy and motor function still require assessment.

PAI can reduce pain and opioid use in pooled comparisons, but the source cautions that medication choice, dose, and volume affect efficacy. Avoid treating a particular mixture as a universal standard.

Multimodal analgesia aims to reduce systemic opioid exposure and associated adverse effects. Evidence for gabapentinoids is mixed, including reports of sedation; select components according to patient factors and the broader care pathway.

Plan for postoperative nausea and vomiting as part of recovery care; the review associates GA with higher rates of postoperative nausea and vomiting but does not establish a specific prophylaxis regimen.

sections.title: Emergence & recovery
bullets: Treat patients as fall risks until neuraxial anesthesia has fully worn off; motor recovery may precede functional balance.
After general anesthesia with neuromuscular blockade, confirm adequate quantitative recovery before extubation; continue recovery care appropriate to the anesthetic and patient condition.
PACU care should include ongoing assessment of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, consciousness, and temperature, with an appropriate handoff and documented recovery status.

sections.title: Neuraxial/deep-block & thromboprophylaxis coordination
bullets: Before neuraxial or deep plexus/peripheral procedures, identify the exact anticoagulant or antiplatelet drug, dose, last administration, renal function and additional bleeding risks. Use current ASRA drug-specific guidance rather than a single interval for every agent.

Coordinate catheter removal and the first postoperative anticoagulant dose before handoff. Surgical hemostasis, dose intensity and neuraxial timing all matter; catheter removal is itself a bleeding-risk event.

Do not stop clinically indicated antithrombotic treatment independently or delay urgent surgery solely to obtain a preferred anesthetic technique. Discuss feasible anesthetic alternatives and the bleeding/thrombosis tradeoff with the treating team.

sections.title: Evidence scope & focused safety supplementation
bullets: The October 7 update supplements this draft with the focused safety references linked in the new sections. These address selected historical review gaps, not every aspect of perioperative care.

Existing procedure reviews remain limited by their study populations, study designs and variable evidence quality. A preference reported in a review is not a mandate for one airway device, anesthetic technique, block or recovery pathway.

Keep source-specific populations distinct: lower-leg compartment guidance is not a universal all-fracture protocol; cemented hemiarthroplasty guidance is not a universal implant-selection rule; a beach-chair safety review does not establish one blood-pressure target for every patient.

Patient-specific decisions, the remaining historical review questions and independent clinical signoff remain open. No universal drug, fluid, transfusion or disposition recipe has been inferred from missing procedure-specific evidence.

sections.title: Monitoring, access & TEE
bullets: Match access and monitoring to ventricular reserve, surgical approach, anticipated bleeding and rescue requirements. Arterial pressure, reliable large-bore access, central access, ECG, temperature and serial blood gases are central to major open cardiac surgery.

TEE evaluates baseline and new ventricular dysfunction, filling, residual structural problems and de-airing. Check contraindications and use an appropriately trained operator; unavailable or contraindicated TEE requires an alternative imaging plan.

A pulmonary artery catheter is selected for the clinical question, not inserted automatically for every case. Interpret pressure, output and oxygenation measurements alongside echo and perfusion rather than treating CVP as a direct volume measurement.

Prepare external defibrillation/pacing capability and vasoactive support before induction. Discuss re-entry, peripheral cannulation and emergency bypass access when prior surgery or circulatory instability makes these relevant.

sections.title: Induction, oxygen delivery & ventricular protection
bullets: Titrate induction to the patient’s reserve and allow time for drug effect in low cardiac output. Avoid a large unopposed fall in vascular tone or contractility while also controlling the tachycardic/hypertensive response to airway instrumentation.

Protect myocardial oxygen supply-demand balance by addressing hypotension, tachycardia, hypoxemia, anemia and new ischemia in context. Blood pressure alone does not establish adequate cardiac output or oxygen delivery.

Use the actual valve or ventricular physiology to choose heart-rate and loading goals. The pressure-loaded LV in aortic stenosis and the volume-loaded LV in regurgitation should not receive an identical hemodynamic recipe.

With pulmonary hypertension or RV dysfunction, prevent avoidable hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis and excessive airway pressure. Balance RV filling against dilatation and septal shift rather than repeatedly giving fluid for every low-output state.

sections.title: Heparin, ACT & protamine
bullets: Establish baseline coagulation, recent antiplatelet/anticoagulant exposure and any HIT history. Confirm adequate anticoagulation before initiating CPB and repeat testing at protocol-defined intervals.

The 2024 European CPB guideline describes ACT >480 seconds for conventional uncoated circuits with cardiotomy suction. Assay and circuit characteristics matter: use the institution’s validated system-specific target, not a universal target copied from PCI, ECMO or another ACT device.

An inadequate ACT response requires confirmation of sampling/testing and an organized heparin-resistance assessment, including antithrombin availability. Acute HIT and alternative anticoagulants require a specialist perfusion/hematology strategy; direct thrombin inhibitors do not have a protamine-like reversal agent.

Coordinate protamine administration with the surgeon and perfusionist after separation. Watch for hypotension, pulmonary vascular/RV deterioration or hypersensitivity and retain a clear emergency return-to-bypass plan.

Persistent bleeding or prolonged ACT after reversal does not prove residual heparin. Temperature, platelets and factor deficits affect testing; excess protamine can itself impair coagulation. Use the cardiac bleeding algorithm and heparin-sensitive testing when available.

sections.title: CPB: perfusion, temperature & laboratory trends
bullets: During bypass, assess pump flow and oxygen delivery together with hemoglobin/hematocrit, venous saturation, gases, lactate and organ-perfusion indicators. A satisfactory pressure reading is not sufficient evidence that tissue oxygen delivery is adequate.

Follow potassium, acid–base status, glucose, calcium as clinically indicated and serial anticoagulation testing. Reconcile anesthetic delivery and ventilation transitions with the perfusionist rather than assuming the usual pre-bypass circuit is still delivering the anesthetic.

Coordinate cooling and controlled rewarming with the perfusion strategy. Avoid systemic hyperthermia; the CPB guideline recommends oxygenator arterial outlet temperature not exceeding 37°C, rather than deliberately heating above normal to qualify for separation.

Treat sudden perfusion or drainage problems as team events. Cannula malposition, obstruction, air, dissection and inadequate venous return require rapid circuit and patient assessment, not isolated escalation of vasoactive drugs.

sections.title: Separation from bypass & low-output differential
bullets: Before reducing support, coordinate ventilation, temperature, rhythm/pacing, electrolyte and acid–base correction, filling and de-airing. Assess the surgical result and both ventricles with TEE.

Distinguish inadequate preload, LV dysfunction, RV failure, ischemia, vasoplegia and a residual structural or dynamic lesion. Similar arterial pressures can conceal very different causes and treatments.

Review new regional wall-motion changes, valve function, intracardiac air and the effect of rhythm/AV synchrony. A postrepair mitral SAM/LVOT-obstruction pattern requires different management from primary pump failure.

Use volume, vasoactive or inotropic treatment for the identified physiology and reassess the response. Avoid forcing separation with escalating high-dose support when inadequate perfusion persists; discuss return to CPB or temporary mechanical support early.

sections.title: Blood conservation & postoperative bleeding
bullets: When time permits, identify and treat preoperative anemia and iron deficiency. Plan crossmatched blood, cell salvage and an institution-approved antifibrinolytic strategy for the expected surgical burden.

Use targeted laboratory/viscoelastic-guided treatment for bleeding while evaluating surgical hemostasis. Correct contributing hypothermia and residual anticoagulation; distinguish a mechanical bleeding source from diffuse coagulopathy.

Restrictive red-cell strategies reduce transfusion in suitable cardiac-surgery patients, but a trial threshold such as 7.5 g/dL is not an instruction to delay transfusion during active hemorrhage, ischemia or inadequate oxygen delivery.

Tranexamic acid is effective in cardiac blood conservation; dosing should account for the local regimen and patient risks, including renal function and seizures. Do not convert an evidence summary into a fixed dose for all procedures.
Postoperative instability with bleeding needs prompt multidisciplinary reassessment. Repeated empiric blood products must not delay evaluation for surgical re-exploration when indicated.

sections.title: Analgesia, extubation & ICU handoff
bullets: Use multimodal analgesia while limiting unnecessary high-dose opioid exposure. Regional techniques require an explicit assessment of systemic anticoagulation, bleeding risk, expertise and the planned postoperative pathway.

NSAIDs are not a routine CABG analgesic option: respect the coronary-revascularization warning/contraindication and renal, bleeding and cardiovascular risks. Do not transfer a VATS analgesic regimen unchanged into CABG.

Fast-track recovery is conditional on stable perfusion, satisfactory gas exchange, temperature, hemostasis, consciousness and neuromuscular recovery. It is not a fixed deadline or a promise of operating-room extubation.

ICU handoff should communicate the operation and residual findings, bypass course, rhythm/pacing, ventricular function, current support, bleeding/transfusion and anticoagulation plan. Continue surveillance for low output, RV dysfunction, vasoplegia, renal injury and respiratory failure.
