overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Confirm configuration and purpose: VV supports respiratory gas exchange; VA adds direct circulatory support.
Use imaging-guided cannulation, a bleeding/vascular-rescue plan and configuration-specific monitoring.
Monitor VV recirculation and gas exchange; with peripheral VA, watch upper-body oxygenation, LV distension and limb perfusion.
Weaning and decannulation require organ-recovery assessment and a specialist trial, not merely improved saturation.

sections.title: VV versus VA support
bullets: VV returns oxygenated blood to the venous circulation and provides no direct hemodynamic support. It may indirectly improve RV function by correcting gas exchange and pulmonary vasoconstriction.
VA returns blood to the arterial circulation and supports perfusion but may increase LV afterload. Central/peripheral and hybrid configurations create different monitoring and rescue needs.

sections.title: Cannulation plan & induction risk
bullets: Clarify urgency, cannulation sites, support already in place and whether the patient can tolerate sedation/induction. Assign cannulation, imaging, perfusion and emergency roles explicitly.
Prepare for hemodynamic changes and occult cannulation bleeding when support begins. Titrate resuscitation to physiology rather than assuming every flow limitation is hypovolemia.

sections.title: Imaging & cannula position
bullets: Use ultrasound for vascular access and appropriate echo/fluoroscopy for guidewire/cannula guidance. Dual-lumen VV positioning particularly requires live imaging; misplaced wires/cannulae can perforate the heart.
Reassess position and drainage/return when flow or oxygenation changes. Secure cannulae and maintain position awareness during transfer and surgery.

sources.label: ELSO: adult VV ECMO guideline

sections.title: VV blood flow, sweep & recirculation
bullets: Blood flow is a major determinant of extracorporeal oxygen delivery; sweep gas primarily controls CO2 removal. Overall oxygenation also depends on hemoglobin, native cardiac output, recirculation and metabolic demand.
Avoid abrupt large reductions in PaCO2 at initiation. Titrate support with serial gases and physiologic assessment.

Recirculation returns oxygenated blood directly to the drainage limb and reduces effective delivery. Worsening saturation despite increased pump flow should prompt assessment, not endless flow escalation.

sources.label: ELSO: adult VV ECMO guideline

sections.title: Peripheral VA: differential oxygenation
bullets: When recovering native cardiac output ejects poorly oxygenated pulmonary venous blood, the upper body may remain hypoxemic despite apparently good lower-body oxygenation.
Right-radial gases/right-hand oximetry help detect this pattern in typical femoral VA configurations. Assess native lung function and discuss configuration changes when refractory.

sources.label: ELSO: adult cardiac VA ECMO interim guideline

sections.title: VA afterload & LV distension
bullets: Assess pulse pressure, aortic-valve opening, LV size/stasis and pulmonary edema. VA flow can increase afterload and impair LV ejection.
Persistent LV distension or pulmonary edema requires specialist unloading assessment. Options depend on physiology and configuration; adjusting flow must preserve organ perfusion.

sources.label: ELSO: adult cardiac VA ECMO interim guideline

sections.title: Distal limb perfusion & vascular injury
bullets: Femoral arterial cannulation can compromise distal flow. Plan distal perfusion and serial clinical/Doppler or NIRS assessment according to configuration and local protocol.
Monitor for bleeding, ischemia, compartment compromise and vascular injury during cannulation and after decannulation. A working circuit does not establish adequate limb perfusion.

sections.title: Anticoagulation, bleeding & thrombosis
bullets: Use the ECMO service’s anticoagulation strategy and serial coagulation/platelet/fibrinogen assessment. CPB ACT targets are not transferable to ECMO.
Life-threatening bleeding may require reducing or holding anticoagulation while closely monitoring thrombosis/circuit risks. Low-flow trials need particular attention to circuit clotting.

sections.title: Lung protection & organ monitoring
bullets: Use lung-protective ventilation while the circuit provides gas exchange; do not reflexively restore injurious ventilator settings for a circuit-related problem.
Follow perfusion, gases, neurologic status, renal function and hemoglobin along with circuit parameters. Thermodilution output may be unreliable during ECMO.

bullets: VV weaning tests native oxygenation and ventilatory reserve through a monitored sweep reduction/off-sweep strategy while preserving safe circuit flow.
VA weaning assesses cardiac recovery and perfusion during a carefully supervised reduction in support, using echo, pressures, gases and vasoactive requirements. A normal EF alone is not sufficient.

Before removal, agree on anticoagulation timing, airway/sedation support, blood availability, vascular closure and postremoval surveillance. Continue assessment for bleeding, thrombosis and limb complications.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Confirm configuration and purpose: VV supports respiratory gas exchange; VA adds direct circulatory support.
Use imaging-guided cannulation, a bleeding/vascular-rescue plan and configuration-specific monitoring.
Monitor VV recirculation and gas exchange; with peripheral VA, watch upper-body oxygenation, LV distension and limb perfusion.
Weaning and decannulation require organ-recovery assessment and a specialist trial, not merely improved saturation.

sections.title: VV versus VA support
bullets: VV returns oxygenated blood to the venous circulation and provides no direct hemodynamic support. It may indirectly improve RV function by correcting gas exchange and pulmonary vasoconstriction.
VA returns blood to the arterial circulation and supports perfusion but may increase LV afterload. Central/peripheral and hybrid configurations create different monitoring and rescue needs.

sources.label: ELSO: adult VV ECMO guideline

sections.title: Cannulation plan & induction risk
bullets: Clarify urgency, cannulation sites, support already in place and whether the patient can tolerate sedation/induction. Assign cannulation, imaging, perfusion and emergency roles explicitly.
Prepare for hemodynamic changes and occult cannulation bleeding when support begins. Titrate resuscitation to physiology rather than assuming every flow limitation is hypovolemia.

sources.label: ELSO: adult VV ECMO guideline

sections.title: Imaging & cannula position
bullets: Use ultrasound for vascular access and appropriate echo/fluoroscopy for guidewire/cannula guidance. Dual-lumen VV positioning particularly requires live imaging; misplaced wires/cannulae can perforate the heart.
Reassess position and drainage/return when flow or oxygenation changes. Secure cannulae and maintain position awareness during transfer and surgery.

sources.label: ELSO: adult VV ECMO guideline

sections.title: VV blood flow, sweep & recirculation
bullets: Blood flow is a major determinant of extracorporeal oxygen delivery; sweep gas primarily controls CO2 removal. Overall oxygenation also depends on hemoglobin, native cardiac output, recirculation and metabolic demand.
Avoid abrupt large reductions in PaCO2 at initiation. Titrate support with serial gases and physiologic assessment.

Recirculation returns oxygenated blood directly to the drainage limb and reduces effective delivery. Worsening saturation despite increased pump flow should prompt assessment, not endless flow escalation.

sources.label: ELSO: adult VV ECMO guideline

sections.title: Peripheral VA: differential oxygenation
bullets: When recovering native cardiac output ejects poorly oxygenated pulmonary venous blood, the upper body may remain hypoxemic despite apparently good lower-body oxygenation.
Right-radial gases/right-hand oximetry help detect this pattern in typical femoral VA configurations. Assess native lung function and discuss configuration changes when refractory.

sources.label: ELSO: adult cardiac VA ECMO interim guideline

sections.title: VA afterload & LV distension
bullets: Assess pulse pressure, aortic-valve opening, LV size/stasis and pulmonary edema. VA flow can increase afterload and impair LV ejection.
Persistent LV distension or pulmonary edema requires specialist unloading assessment. Options depend on physiology and configuration; adjusting flow must preserve organ perfusion.

sources.label: ELSO: adult cardiac VA ECMO interim guideline

sections.title: Distal limb perfusion & vascular injury
bullets: Femoral arterial cannulation can compromise distal flow. Plan distal perfusion and serial clinical/Doppler or NIRS assessment according to configuration and local protocol.
Monitor for bleeding, ischemia, compartment compromise and vascular injury during cannulation and after decannulation. A working circuit does not establish adequate limb perfusion.

sources.label: ELSO: adult cardiac VA ECMO interim guideline

sections.title: Anticoagulation, bleeding & thrombosis
bullets: Use the ECMO service’s anticoagulation strategy and serial coagulation/platelet/fibrinogen assessment. CPB ACT targets are not transferable to ECMO.
Life-threatening bleeding may require reducing or holding anticoagulation while closely monitoring thrombosis/circuit risks. Low-flow trials need particular attention to circuit clotting.

Do not equate ACT, aPTT and anti-Xa or escalate heparin from one discordant result alone. A 2025 VV-ECMO review describes inflammation/factor effects on aPTT and hemolysis, bilirubin or lipemia interference with chromogenic assays; review assay method and clinical context with the ECMO team/laboratory.

Interpret anticoagulation alongside bleeding, platelets/fibrinogen, circuit thrombus, circuit performance and patient perfusion. No single assay predicts every bleeding or thrombotic complication; direct-thrombin-inhibitor monitoring has additional assay limitations.

The review is VV-focused and is not a universal VA-ECMO target table. Anticoagulation interruption and resumption during bleeding or decannulation remain ECMO-service decisions with explicit circuit/patient thrombosis surveillance.

overview.title: Quick clinical overview
bullets: Define the operation and urgency first: short vaginal instrumentation, prolonged laparoscopy, or major open pelvic resection require different plans.
Assess aspiration, pregnancy possibility, anemia/bleeding, cardiopulmonary reserve and expected access restrictions.
Prioritize lithotomy nerve protection, Trendelenburg/CO₂ physiology, blood readiness and hysteroscopic fluid tracking when applicable.
Plan opioid-sparing analgesia, PONV prevention, safe emergence, urinary care, VTE prevention and the appropriate recovery location.

sections.title: Pneumoperitoneum & Trendelenburg physiology
bullets: CO₂ insufflation and head-down positioning reduce FRC/compliance, increase airway pressures and CO₂ load, and alter SVR and venous return. Cardiac output responses depend on insufflation pressure, position, volume status and ventricular reserve; decreases are not inevitable in every patient.

Use lung-protective tidal volumes based on predicted body weight, individualize PEEP and minute ventilation, and reassess ETT depth after positioning. Sudden bradycardia with insufflation requires communication, stopping the stimulus/deflation and treatment; unexplained hypoxemia or collapse warrants evaluation for hemorrhage, gas embolism or thoracic gas complications.

sources.label: OpenAnesthesia: laparoscopic and robotic surgery (2024 educational review)

sections.title: Hemorrhage recognition & resuscitation
bullets: For substantial anticipated bleeding, establish suitable access, type/crossmatch and a blood-delivery plan before incision. During active hemorrhage activate the local pathway early, follow perfusion and serial laboratory trends, and address hypothermia, hypocalcemia, fibrinogen/platelet deficits and coagulopathy as indicated.

A normal initial hemoglobin does not exclude acute major blood loss. Resuscitation and definitive surgical control proceed together; vasopressors may support perfusion but do not replace blood or correction of the bleeding source.

sections.title: Procedure families & boundaries
bullets: Use the procedure-specific reference rather than assuming all gynecologic cases need GA, steep Trendelenburg or a blood crossmatch. Local/MAC or neuraxial techniques may suit selected brief vaginal procedures; laparoscopy commonly requires controlled ventilation and a secured airway.

Cesarean delivery and postpartum hemorrhage remain in Obstetrics. Existing cerclage and postpartum tubal-ligation routes are retained as related pregnancy/postpartum procedures; this expansion does not replace those references.

sections.title: Preoperative assessment & optimization
bullets: Confirm indication, approach, pregnancy possibility and testing with consent under local policy. Review anemia, bleeding history, anticoagulants, obesity/OSA, cardiopulmonary reserve, renal function, prior pelvic operations and baseline neurologic symptoms.

Investigate and treat iron-deficiency anemia and nutritional deficits before elective major surgery when time permits. Urgent hemorrhage or source control should not wait for completion of an elective optimization pathway.

sections.title: Anesthetic technique & aspiration assessment
bullets: Choose local anesthesia with or without sedation, neuraxial anesthesia or GA according to procedure, duration, patient preference and rescue needs. MAC is an anesthesia service, not a fixed depth; sedation can progress to apnea and requires airway-rescue capability.

Assess vomiting, pain/opioids, reflux, obstruction, fasting and gestational stage individually. Early pregnancy alone does not establish delayed gastric emptying or mandate identical full-stomach management for every patient; active vomiting, shock or an emergency may still justify a protected-airway/rapid-sequence strategy.

sections.title: Monitoring, access & thermal care
bullets: Use appropriate ECG, blood pressure, oxygenation and ventilation monitoring; exhaled CO₂ is expected during moderate/deep sedation unless precluded or invalidated. Monitor temperature when clinically significant changes are intended, anticipated or suspected.

Match venous access, arterial monitoring and blood availability to hemorrhage risk and physiologic reserve, not the procedure name alone. Warm patients and substantial fluid/blood infusions; reassess hemoglobin, electrolytes, glucose and acid-base status as indicated.

sources.label: ASA Standards for Basic Anesthetic Monitoring

sections.title: Lithotomy, pressure points & nerve protection
bullets: Document mobility limits and neuropathy; lift and lower legs together with adequate personnel. Protect the fibular head, heels and calves, avoid excessive hip flexion/abduction or external rotation, and avoid traction/compression on the brachial plexus or tucked arms.

Minimize time in lithotomy and steep Trendelenburg, reassess supports and perfusion when feasible, and avoid prolonged hypotension or concentrated calf pressure. Severe postoperative leg pain, swelling or weakness can signal compartment syndrome even with palpable pulses; obtain urgent assessment rather than attributing it automatically to a block.

sources.label: DGGG/OEGGG/SGGG positioning consensus (2020/2021; stated validity ended July 2025)

sections.title: Perfusion, blood loss & fluid balance
bullets: Target euvolemia with reassessment of perfusion and measured losses; avoid both indiscriminate crystalloid loading and rigid restriction during bleeding. Distinguish vasodilation from hypovolemia or low cardiac output before choosing fluid, blood or vasoactive support.

Account for poor intake, bowel preparation, ascites drainage and irrigation absorption when relevant. Oliguria during pneumoperitoneum or pelvic manipulation is not by itself a mandate for repeated fluid boluses; inspect the catheter, hemodynamics and surgical context.

sources.label: Gynecologic oncology ERAS implementation review (2021; summarizes 2016/2019 guidance)
ERAS Society vulvar and vaginal surgery recommendations (2020)

sections.title: Analgesia & PONV prevention
bullets: Use multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia with acetaminophen and an NSAID when renal function, bleeding risk and other contraindications permit. Local infiltration or an appropriate regional block may reduce incisional pain; blocks do not reliably eliminate visceral pelvic pain.

Assess PONV risk and use multimodal prophylaxis from different drug classes when indicated; consider propofol-based anesthesia and opioid reduction. Choose rescue antiemetics from a different class where possible and account for QT risk, sedation, urinary retention and other patient-specific effects.

sources.label: ERAS gynecologic oncology implementation update (2023; not the 2026 update)

sections.title: Emergence, airway safety & disposition
bullets: Before extubation, confirm consciousness, airway protection, gas exchange, temperature and hemodynamic stability. After neuromuscular blockade verify quantitative TOF ratio at least 0.9 at the adductor pollicis; prolonged Trendelenburg also requires assessment for airway edema and a safe reintubation plan.

Arrange observation or higher-acuity care for persistent shock, major bleeding, airway swelling or respiratory compromise. Discharge requires controlled pain/nausea, appropriate bleeding assessment and procedure-specific voiding/catheter and return-precaution plans.

sections.title: VTE prevention & postoperative recovery
bullets: Assess cancer, prior VTE, obesity, immobility and bleeding risk. Coordinate mechanical and pharmacologic prophylaxis with surgical hemostasis, renal function and neuraxial timing; do not apply an automatic anticoagulant hold/restart schedule.

After major open pelvic cancer surgery, evaluate extended prophylaxis under the oncology pathway; the 2023 ERAS update supports 28 days in high-risk patients, not routine extension for every minor or minimally invasive case. Mobilize and resume nutrition as feasible, with exceptions for instability or specific reconstruction requirements.

bullets: A 2026 ERAS gynecologic oncology update is listed by the ERAS Society. On October 7, its publisher full text could not be verified because automated access was blocked and the browser presented a robot challenge.

The existing ERAS recommendations remain attributed to the accessible 2023/earlier sources. Do not describe this specialty as reconciled with the 2026 update until the full recommendations are obtained, compared and reviewed.
